Skydance Says Paramount and Warner Bros. Will Not Bid Against Each Other
Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said the merged studios will "coordinate and align and not compete directly," and Puck reports Barbie 2 talks have restarted at Warner Bros.
Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said at the company's Oct. 6 press conference that Paramount and Warner Bros. will "coordinate and align and not compete directly." Matthew Belloni reports in Puck that Skydance plans to decide internally which part of the company takes a project before bidding raises its cost. That removes one bidder when a filmmaker auctions a film or a showrunner shops an overall deal. Kreiz said release dates will also be set by genre and audience across both studios. Belloni reports Barbie 2 talks have restarted and that HBO Max is buying aggressively.
Potential Talent Implication: Paramount and Warner Bros. used to be two separate bids on a Nolan film or a showrunner's overall deal, and Skydance now plans to put in one, leaving Netflix, Disney, Universal, Sony and Amazon as the other bidders.
The Facts
  • Kreiz, Oct. 6 press conference: "In the sense that the company is still one platform, we will coordinate and align and not compete directly."
  • Kreiz on releases: "We will choreograph the release schedule to optimize by genre, by audience demographic, to achieve the best for the company as a whole."
  • Puck (Skydance sources): the company hopes to decide internally which projects suit which studio "before artificially pushing up their costs."
  • Examples Belloni cites: a Christopher Nolan film auction; overall deals for Mindy Kaling, Bill Lawrence or Quinta Brunson shopped to Warner Bros. Television and Paramount Television Studios.
  • Dating overlaps Belloni flags: A Minecraft Movie sequel (Warner Bros.) and A Quiet Place III (Paramount) on successive weekends next July; Sonic the Hedgehog 4 (Paramount) and Godzilla x Kong: Supernova (Warner Bros.) in March.
  • Barbie 2: talks have restarted (Puck); Belloni expects an announcement in weeks.
  • HBO Max subscribers about 140 million, Paramount+ about 80 million; Kreiz said the services will run separately for now.
  • Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein are reviewing the Warner Bros. slate left by Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy; they met production president Jesse Ehrman and co-head Mikey Ireland on Oct. 6.
  • Disclosure in the piece: RedBird Capital is an investor in both Skydance and Puck.
· Puck · Matthew Belloni · 2026-10-09 · https://puck.news/skydance-questions-what-hollywood-most-wants-to-know/ · Provenance: named-exec-quote source ↗
Netflix Creator Deals Keep Videos on YouTube and Off Every Other Streamer
LightShed estimates Netflix has committed upward of $1 billion to creators, mostly on three-year deals that let videos stay on YouTube but bar them from rival streamers.
LightShed Partners estimates Netflix has committed upward of $1 billion across mostly three-year creator and video podcast deals, out of a $20 billion annual content budget. The deals reportedly let creators keep posting on YouTube while barring the same content from other streaming services. LightShed reports YouTube has privately warned creators who work with Netflix that they risk YouTube-arranged brand deals, marketing placement, executive access and possibly YouTube Preferred, its premium ad tier. Cocomelon leaves Netflix for Disney+ in January 2027 after Netflix declined to renew.
Potential Talent Implication: A Netflix creator deal reportedly leaves the videos on YouTube but locks out Disney+, Hulu and every other streamer for the term, and Cocomelon, whose license Netflix declined to renew, shows the check may not come back.
The Facts
  • Netflix creator spend (LightShed estimate, "we hear"): upward of $1 billion committed, mostly three-year deals spanning video podcasts and creator content; Netflix content budget about $20 billion a year.
  • Deal terms (reported): creator content may stay on YouTube; the same content is barred from other streaming services.
  • YouTube's private warnings to creators working with Netflix (LightShed): possible loss of YouTube-arranged brand deals, less promotion (billboards, Brandcast), less access to senior executives, possible removal from YouTube Preferred.
  • Neal Mohan to The Wall Street Journal: "A creator's posting strategy has implications."
  • YouTube has begun offering top creators low seven figures to about $10 million for first-window exclusivity (Bloomberg and The Ankler, cited by LightShed).
  • Creators now on Netflix: Good Mythical Morning, Mark Rober, Therapuss, Stokes Twins, Salish and Jordan Matter, Chicken Shop Date, Sam and Colby.
  • Jay Shetty moved his video podcasts exclusively to Netflix and Spotify; audio stays everywhere.
  • Cocomelon leaves Netflix for Disney+ in January 2027 after Netflix declined to renew.
  • Scale: YouTube had 14.2% of U.S. TV viewing in July (Nielsen), nearly double Netflix; YouTube ad revenue $43 billion over 12 months; Netflix advertising about $3 billion.
  • Obsession (Curry Barker) and Backrooms (Kane Parsons) have each grossed more than $300 million worldwide.

An AI Voice in a Royal Mail Ad Matches a Dead BBC Narrator, and His Family Was Never Asked
Royal Mail admitted its 2025 Christmas ad used an AI narrator built on ElevenLabs technology; a University of York phonetics professor found considerable similarity to Paul Vaughan, who died in 2014.
Royal Mail confirmed to Deadline that its 2025 Christmas campaign used an AI-generated narrator in place of a voiceover artist. Lucy Wynne recognized the voice as her father, Paul Vaughan, narrator of the BBC's Horizon, Threads and Paddington audiobooks. Czech company Fameplay made the voice with licensed ElevenLabs technology and says no Vaughan reference went into its prompts. ElevenLabs said it was not a direct clone and declined to say whether its model trained on his recordings. A forensic speech professor and three open-source tools found strong similarity. ElevenLabs has since added Vaughan to its No Go Voices list.
Potential Talent Implication: Nobody cloned Paul Vaughan on purpose, yet a model working from generic prompts produced a voice his daughter and a forensic phonetician both matched to him, and the only remedy so far is ElevenLabs adding his name to a blocklist.
The Facts
  • Ad: Royal Mail 2025 Christmas campaign "so much more than just a card," aired on ITV from November 2025; agency Darwin & the Machines; human scenes produced by Untold Studios with UK actors.
  • Voice: subcontracted to Fameplay (Czechia), which licenses ElevenLabs technology. Fameplay is backed by Czech Media Invest, chaired by Daniel Kretinsky, whose EP Group owns Royal Mail.
  • Royal Mail: the voiceover was "not designed to replicate any specific individual"; producers "carried out checks and advised that these did not identify any resemblance concerns"; AI voiceover is "increasingly common."
  • ElevenLabs: confirmed the narration was not a direct voice clone of Vaughan; declined to comment on whether its model trained on his recordings; added Vaughan to its No Go Voices list.
  • Vincent Hughes, professor of forensic speech science, University of York: "considerable phonetic similarity." Three open-source analysis tools judged a good chance of "same speaker."
  • Paul Vaughan: voice of BBC's Horizon and Radio 4's Kaleidoscope, narrator of Threads, Paddington audiobooks; died 11 years before the ad aired.
  • Lucy Wynne: "It's outrageous." No apology received from Royal Mail.
  • Peter Caulfield, founder of the Save Our Voices Now campaign: using AI "without thorough checks, can result in a company stealing a voice from the grave."

Netflix Is Preparing Its Biggest Layoff Since 2022, About 5% of Staff
Cuts of about 5% of roughly 17,000 employees could come as soon as next week, Puck reports; Netflix shares are down more than 40% over the past year.
Netflix is preparing layoffs of about 5% of its workforce, Matthew Belloni reports in Puck, citing sources; at roughly 17,000 employees that is about 850 jobs. Deadline reports the cuts could start as early as Friday or next week. Netflix declined to comment to Puck and did not respond to Deadline. Its last large cut, in 2022, affected about 150 people. Deadline reports engagement rose 2% in the first half. Ted Sarandos said last week the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to." Earnings are Oct. 20.
Potential Talent Implication: Netflix is cutting staff over 2% engagement growth and a stock down more than 40%, and its buyers may now judge a pitch on the viewing hours it can add more than on what it costs.
The Facts
  • Size: about 5% of employees (Puck, sources); Netflix employed about 17,000 at last estimate, so about 850 jobs.
  • Timing: as early as next week (Puck); as early as Friday, Oct. 9, or next week (Deadline).
  • Netflix: declined to comment (Puck); did not respond (Deadline).
  • Prior cuts: about 150 employees, about 2% of staff, in 2022; several dozen in the product division in February 2026.
  • Stock: down more than 40% over the past year (Deadline); under pressure since the failed bid for Warner Bros. (Puck).
  • Engagement: up 2% in the first half of 2026 (Deadline).
  • Sarandos at the Bloomberg Screentime conference: "Overall, we're not growing as fast as I want us to, and we're working on making that move faster."
  • Q3 earnings: Oct. 20, 2026.

Sony Hands Screen Gems to a YouTube Executive to Build Creator Movies
Sony named former YouTube executive Fede Goldenberg to run Screen Gems on Friday, with a mandate for theatrical films from digital-native creators; Ashley Brucks moves to a producing role.
Sony Pictures named Fede Goldenberg, a former YouTube executive with 15 years of creator relationships, to lead Screen Gems, reporting to Motion Picture Group president Sanford Panitch. The label will focus on theatrical films, not streaming, from short-form and long-form creators. TheWrap points to Curry Barker's Obsession ($522 million worldwide) and Kane Parsons' Backrooms ($400 million), and notes Markiplier's self-financed, self-released Iron Lung made $50 million. A Sony insider said independent creator releases often lack global release and marketing plans, the gap Screen Gems intends to fill.
Potential Talent Implication: Markiplier self-financed and self-released Iron Lung to $50 million, and Sony now has a label whose stated job is the global release and marketing that route lacked, a pitch aimed at creators who guard their IP.
The Facts
  • Hire: Fede Goldenberg, former YouTube executive (15 years working with creators, part of the YouTube Originals era, involved in YouTube acquiring the Oscars), named head of Screen Gems Pictures on Friday, Oct. 9. Reports to Sanford Panitch, president of Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group.
  • Ashley Brucks, Screen Gems president since 2023, transitions to a producing role.
  • Mandate: theatrical projects from digital-native storytellers, short-form and long-form; theatrical rather than streaming, although Sony has a streaming deal with Netflix.
  • Box office cited by TheWrap: Obsession (Focus Features, Curry Barker) $522 million on a budget under $1 million; Backrooms (Kane Parsons) $400 million; Iron Lung (Markiplier) $50 million, self-financed and self-released.
  • Godmother: Jacksepticeye personally financed principal photography; Helmstreet Productions funded post-production.
  • Screen Gems results cited: Until Dawn $54 million on $15 million; I Know What You Did Last Summer $65 million on $18 million; Evil Dead Burn $72 million on $20 million; Insidious: Out of the Further $170 million on $18 million.
  • Sony insider (unnamed): independent creator releases often lack global release plans or robust marketing plans.
  • RJ Larese, president of creator agency Sixteenth, on the hire: creators are becoming part of who shapes where Hollywood goes next.

Coppola Keeps Megalopolis Off U.S. Streaming and Takes It Back to Theaters
Reading International will show Megalopolis in theaters on October 24 with a live Q&A with Francis Ford Coppola, who self-financed the film and barred it from U.S. streaming services and DVD.
Deadline reports exclusively that Megalopolis returns to theaters for the first time since its 2024 launch, booked by Reading International in cinemas across the country for a simultaneous screening on October 24, followed by a livestreamed Q&A with Francis Ford Coppola moderated by his son Roman. Coppola decided when he self-financed and shot the film that it would not go through domestic streaming services or U.S. DVDs. Deadline says the film became one of the most expensive independent films ever. Coppola plans periodic returns, including a New Year's Day screening each year.
Potential Talent Implication: Coppola self-financed Megalopolis and kept it off U.S. streaming and DVD, so he alone decides when and where it plays, and what he has chosen is event screenings he can host live.
The Facts
  • Booking: Reading International Inc. in many of its cinemas, from New York to Hawaii, screening simultaneously Oct. 24, including Village East Cinemas in New York City.
  • Format: livestreamed Q&A with Coppola, moderated by Roman Coppola; audiences text questions before, during and after the film. Each audience member gets a hard-copy letter with Coppola's director's statement; the "Live Element" returns.
  • Windowing: Coppola decided at financing that the film would not go to any domestic-based streaming service or U.S. DVD. Deadline: he felt it was now time to put it back out.
  • Future: periodic theatrical returns, including a screening each New Year's Day.
  • Budget context (Deadline): Coppola spent a fortune to stake the film personally; one of the most expensive indies ever.
  • Cast: Adam Driver, Shia LaBeouf, Dustin Hoffman, Jon Voight, Nathalie Emmanuel, Laurence Fishburne, Aubrey Plaza, Giancarlo Esposito.
  • Coppola quote: "Megalopolis is back in its rightful place, theaters, and the interest in seeing it as was intended is growing."

Five Warner Bros. Discovery Executives Collected More Than $1.1 Billion From the Sale
SEC filings show David Zaslav collected more than $600 million and four deputies $90 million to $150 million each when Paramount closed its $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery this week.
According to SEC filings reported by Deadline, five top Warner Bros. Discovery executives took more than $1.1 billion in merger-related pay when Paramount, renamed Skydance, closed its $110 billion acquisition on October 6. David Zaslav collected more than $600 million, with his stock exchanged at $31 a share and his options vesting at closing. JB Perrette, Gunnar Wiedenfels and Bruce Campbell each received $120 million to $150 million, and Gerhard Zeiler about $90 million. Perrette, who stays at Skydance, could defer his payout. A company representative said nearly half of the 35,500 employees held equity at closing.
Potential Talent Implication: The sale paid out through stock and options that vested at closing, more than $1.1 billion to five executives and more than $1 million of equity each to about 500 employees.
The Facts
  • Deal: Paramount (renamed Skydance) closed its $110 billion acquisition of WBD on Oct. 6; WBD holders received $31 a share.
  • Zaslav: more than $600 million (Deadline, Oct. 8: just over $600 million from stock and options; the figure exceeds the roughly $517 million first anticipated). His package also includes a $34.2 million cash bonus, $44.2 million in perquisites and an unspecified tax reimbursement.
  • JB Perrette, Gunnar Wiedenfels, Bruce Campbell: $120 million to $150 million each. Gerhard Zeiler: about $90 million. Combined with Zaslav, more than $1.1 billion.
  • Others: Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar (joined Feb. 2025) more than $57 million; Ken Lowe $18.1 million; Samuel Di Piazza $3.1 million; Debra Lee $1.3 million.
  • Caveats: Perrette could defer his payout because he remains at Skydance; payouts are subject to taxes; options vest on varying schedules; several executives sold shares earlier.
  • Employee equity: nearly half of 35,500 employees held equity at closing, up from about 8,500 in 2022; about 500 employees hold more than $1 million each (New York Post, cited by Deadline).
  • Offer history: Paramount's first offer was $18 a share; WBD accepted Netflix's $27.75 for studios and streaming before finalizing with Paramount.
  • Deadline: only the Endeavor Group IPO and privatization rivals the merger for executive pay tied to an M&A deal.

Artists Equity Pays Its Writers, Directors and Actors Like Equity Investors, and Netflix Shares the Data
Ben Affleck told Variety that Artists Equity shares all streaming revenue with writers, directors, actors and producers on top of fees, and negotiated Netflix bonuses that pay a film's entire crew.
In a Variety cover interview published Oct. 7, Ben Affleck described how Artists Equity, formed in 2022 by Affleck, Matt Damon and RedBird Capital's Gerry Cardinale, pays talent. Writers, directors, actors and producers are "compensated exactly as equity financiers would be," Affleck said. Variety reports the company shares all streaming revenue with them in addition to fees, and negotiated performance bonuses with Netflix that pay a film's entire crew. Affleck said Netflix agreed to share information on what succeeds on its platform, that the model began with Air at Amazon, and that "People got bonuses."
Potential Talent Implication: Affleck and Damon got Netflix to share its performance data and pay bonuses off it, which gives any producer with a Netflix deal a precedent for asking who sees the numbers behind a bonus.
The Facts
  • Artists Equity: founded 2022 by Ben Affleck and Matt Damon with RedBird Capital's Gerry Cardinale; Variety calls it the leading outside producer of Netflix original films (first-look deal to produce films for the service). Netflix acquired Affleck's AI startup InterPositive in July for nearly $590 million in cash.
  • Model (Variety): shares all streaming revenue with above-the-line talent (screenwriters, directors, actors, producers) in addition to traditional fees; negotiated performance-based bonuses with Netflix that pay the entire crew of a film.
  • Affleck: "We seek to compensate old-school above the line talent... as if they were investors in a film. It works on the clean, evident construction that those parties are compensated exactly as equity financiers would be. Not in some kind of arcane, separate bonus pool."
  • Affleck: "Netflix was willing to share some information about what's successful on their platform." "We've had success. People got bonuses."
  • Origin: started with Air at Amazon; The Rip at Netflix cited as another example. Partnerships named: Netflix and Sony.
  • Also: Artists Equity Independent Pictures, an indie theatrical film fund for next-generation filmmakers (filed 10/7). Next release: Animals (Affleck directs and stars; Kerry Washington, Steven Yeun, Gillian Anderson).

Xbox Now Runs Its Own Film, Merchandise and Theme Park Business for Minecraft, Halo and Call of Duty
Xbox formed XP under Mojang president Kayleen Walters, an executive producer of A Minecraft Movie, to run film and TV, licensing, sponsorships and live events for its game franchises.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced XP on Oct. 8, a division with four units: Xbox Pictures for film and TV adaptations, Xbox Products for licensing and merchandise, Xbox Partnerships for sponsors and Xbox Places for events, theme parks and location-based experiences. Kayleen Walters leads it; she spent 13 years at Lucasfilm, grew Minecraft consumer products to more than 250 licensees, and produced A Minecraft Movie and its sequel. The franchises include Minecraft, Call of Duty, Fallout, Warcraft, Halo and Candy Crush. Current adaptations include Amazon's Fallout, a Diablo animated series and a Call of Duty film at Paramount.
Potential Talent Implication: A producer bringing Minecraft or Fallout to the screen now negotiates with an owner that runs its own merchandise, sponsorship and theme-park lines, which may make the producer's share of those lines the term that decides the deal.
The Facts
  • XP ("experience points") announced Oct. 8, 2026 by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma (memo on Xbox Wire); chief strategy officer Matthew Ball outlined the vision to staff.
  • Four units: XBOX PICTURES (film and TV adaptations), XBOX PRODUCTS (licensing and merchandise), XBOX PARTNERSHIPS (sponsors, brand partners), XBOX PLACES (broadcast and in-person events, theme parks, location-based experiences).
  • President: Kayleen Walters, previously president of Mojang; 13 years at Lucasfilm; grew Minecraft consumer products into "a multibillion-dollar business with more than 250 licensees"; executive producer of A Minecraft Movie (biggest U.S. film of 2025 per Sharma; top five worldwide) and a producer of the sequel. The Facts
  • Radford Studio Center (Studio City): Hackman Capital paid nearly $2 billion in 2021, largely debt-financed; ViacomCBS sold it to Hackman and Square Mile Capital for $1.85 billion.   • Netflix is "closing in on a deal at about a fifth of that price" (THR).
  • Four of Hackman's five major L.A. studio properties are being shopped, including Television City. An unnamed source: "In L.A., I think it's a curtain call for Hackman."
  • Property tax appeals since 2020 by the companies controlling the major lots: 269 appeals, about $319 million clawed back in decided cases; Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, Universal and Sony account for more than $245 million.

Paramount won about $15.6 million across 14 appeals.

  • Warner Bros. lot occupancy last year: 91 percent. Simon Robinson, president of global experiences and studio operations: "We were at highs effectively for all of last year."
  • New supply: East End Studios' $230 million Mission Campus (January); Cinespace six-stage Woodland Hills facility (March); Echelon, $450 million, opening later this year; FilmLA tracks seven more planned builds or renovations.

Underlying Rights Holders, Not Skydance, Decide Whether Its Franchises Can Cross Over
J.K. Rowling, Hasbro and the Tolkien estate hold the licenses behind Harry Potter, Transformers and Lord of the Rings, and IndieWire found merger-assignment language in the licensing contracts it reviewed.
IndieWire reports that the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger does not let Skydance combine its biggest franchises, because many were licensed from outside owners. Warner Bros. would need J.K. Rowling's sign-off to put her characters in another franchise; Hasbro controls Transformers; Lord of the Rings rests on a license with the Tolkien estate. Law professors Rachel Landy and Orly Ravid said the original contracts set the limits. IndieWire reviewed licenses that reassign rights to "any entity with which [the] company is merged," so creators cannot use the change of owner to take characters back.
Potential Talent Implication: Rowling, Hasbro and the Tolkien estate kept approval over where their characters can appear, so a $111 billion merger still cannot put Harry Potter beside Optimus Prime; the assignment clause in a license decides who the creator works for after the next sale.
The Facts
  • Skydance closed its $111 billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery this week; Ellison emphasized the combined IP at the press conference on the Warner lot.
  • Rachel Landy (Cardozo School of Law): wholly original Warner Bros. material is likely 100 percent owned and transferable; much of the marquee slate is based on books, comics, toys and dolls licensed from underlying rights holders.
  • Harry Potter: Warner Bros. can keep making films and shows but would need J.K. Rowling's sign-off to put her characters in another franchise.
  • Transformers: controlled by Hasbro. Lord of the Rings: Warner Bros. adapts under "an often contentious licensing agreement" with the Tolkien estate. Star Trek: owned outright by Paramount via the 2019 CBS merger, but not the subsequent films.
  • Orly Ravid (Southwestern Law School): "Many of the underlying rights holders negotiated for lots of protections."
  • Batman is owned outright by Warner Bros. through DC Comics; Mission: Impossible is owned by Paramount via its 1968 purchase of Desilu. Insiders at both studios dismissed live-action crossovers; one executive cited animation (The LEGO Movie model) as a possible exception.
  • No consultation needed: Warner Bros. controls Tom & Jerry, Bugs Bunny and Superman via Hanna-Barbera and DC; Paramount created Top Gun, Dora the Explorer and SpongeBob SquarePants.
  • Nearly every licensing deal includes language reassigning rights to "any entity with which [the] company is merged" (IndieWire reviewed examples).
  • 2022 precedent: Brian Robbins needed sign-off from Steven Spielberg, Hasbro and Michael Bay for the G.I. Joe coda in Transformers: Rise of the Beasts; Paramount has since dropped the Transformers and G.I. Joe crossover.
  • Landy: "Paramount has done a lot of diligence to ensure that they can exploit what they want to exploit or the deal isn't worth it."

  • Moody's (Sept. 29): Ba3. S&P Global (Oct. 2): net-debt-to-adjusted-earnings of about 7x in 2026 and 2027; target 3x or less by 2029.

Training AI on a Film's Own Footage Still Runs Into the Actors' Contracts
Puck's Eriq Gardner argues InterPositive's pitch of models trained only on a production's own dailies does not clear the performers' rights embedded in that footage.
Ben Affleck sold his AI company InterPositive to Netflix for a reported $600 million; it trains models on a production's own dailies and sells the results as "clean." Puck legal columnist Eriq Gardner argues a studio can own the footage without owning the right to train on the performances in it, because actors' contracts and union agreements often do not clearly authorize machine-learning training. The same question applies to cinematographers, stunt performers, choreographers and composers. He expects guild grievances, contract disputes, and chain-of-title (proof of ownership) and insurance fights over AI-assisted work.
Potential Talent Implication: An actor's contract that is silent on machine-learning training leaves the performance in the dailies open to a studio's own-footage model, and every training license that gets signed adds evidence that those rights carry a price.
The Facts
  • Affleck, at Bloomberg's Screentime conference, said he used AI for "lots of things" on his Netflix film Animals and declined to give specifics; he sold InterPositive to Netflix for a reported $600 million.
  • InterPositive's pitch: outputs are "clean" because the model is trained on a film's own dailies.
  • Gardner: training a model "on our own stuff" is not the same as owning or having cleared every right the training implicates. Studios may own the footage and distribution rights, but performers' contracts and collective bargaining agreements often do not specifically authorize training "to create a new generation of synthetic performers."
  • Gardner: a public company making sweeping claims about airtight AI practices could invite a securities suit if the rights picture proves messier.
  • Gardner on licensing: the more companies license copyrighted material, the stronger the evidence that a market for training rights exists, which could make the fair-use defense harder over time.
  • Context: The New York Times v. Microsoft and OpenAI is at summary judgment; Anthropic paid $1.5 billion to settle with authors; Jeffrey Katzenberg has argued for a consent-and-credit model tied to Reactor, a generative video platform he invested in.

Germany's Production Incentive Money Ran Out in August, and Next Year's Pot Is Smaller
The DFFF and GMPF used up their €250 million for 2026 after 230 applications; waiting projects move to 2027, when the government proposes cutting the budget to €200 million.
The German Federal Film Board (FFA) told FilmFest Hamburg's Industry Days that the €250 million budget for Germany's two automatic production incentives, the German Federal Film Fund (DFFF) and the German Motion Picture Fund (GMPF), ran out in August. Applications ran 40% above the level before the rebate rose from 25% to 30% of approved German spend in 2025. Approved but unfunded projects carry into 2027, when the coalition proposes cutting the budget to €200 million, with up to €70 million reserved for features. Separately, Flanders will abolish its €3.5 million Screen Flanders fund on January 1, 2027.

The Facts

Skydance Will Run All of 2027 Without Free Cash Flow
S&P, Moody's and CreditSights put Skydance at nearly $80 billion of debt and seven times earnings, with negative cash flow projected for 2027 and Larry Ellison backstopping the 2028 and 2029 leverage targets.
Skydance, the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery that formally closes October 6, starts with nearly $80 billion of debt, against about $53 billion when WBD formed in 2022. S&P Global puts leverage at seven times earnings in 2026 and 2027, with a target of three or less by 2029; if the company misses its lender targets, Larry Ellison covers the gap personally. Analysts project negative cash flow for all of 2027 and say the promised $6 billion of savings will come largely from staff cuts. Linear networks still deliver more than 70% of profit.
Potential Talent Implication: Skydance enters 2027 with no projected free cash flow and leverage targets Larry Ellison must cover personally if they are missed; upfront guarantees on projects there may be the hardest money to get until those targets are met.
The Facts
  • Debt: nearly $80 billion at close (Variety). Comparison: WBD had about $53 billion of gross debt as of June 2022 after assuming $43 billion from AT&T.
  • Close: formally set for October 6, 2026; the combined company is named Skydance.
  • Leverage: S&P Global and others calculate debt-to-earnings of 7 in 2026 and 2027; goal of 3 or less by 2029.
  • Backstop: if lender leverage targets for the end of 2028 and 2029 are missed, Larry Ellison makes up the difference from personal wealth.
  • Ratings: Moody's Ba3 (one notch below investment grade); S&P Global and CreditSights rate slightly higher, at investment grade.
  • Cash flow: projected negative for all of 2027 (Variety; S&P's Jawad Hussain: "2027 is not going to have any cash flow").
  • Savings: $6 billion of operational savings committed over three years, much of it from staff cuts.
  • Linear networks (CNN, TNT, TBS, Discovery, Nickelodeon, CBS): "70%-plus of the profits and almost all the free cash flow" (CreditSights' Hunter Martin).
  • Cost of the 12-state antitrust suit: probably another $500 million in higher interest on short-term debt (Martin).
  • Financing (Paramount Skydance IR, Sept. 30, 2026): priced $41.4 billion and EUR 885 million of senior secured notes and an $8.5 billion and EUR 850 million Term Loan B, including 6.30% senior secured first lien notes due 2028.
  • MoffettNathanson's Robert Fishman: "The company is going to be forced into choosing where to invest their dollars, led by streaming."

A Judge Threw Out Penske's Antitrust Case Over Google's AI Summaries of Its Articles
Judge Amit Mehta ruled that a publisher's expectation of search traffic is not an agreement; Penske, which owns Variety, Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter, can refile because the dismissal was without prejudice.
U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Penske Media's suit against Google over AI Overviews, ruling Wednesday that antitrust law does not apply, TheWrap reports. Penske argued Google unlawfully conditions inclusion in search results on letting its articles feed AI summaries, said it lost revenue, and asked that Google be required to pay publishers to summarize articles or train AI on them. Mehta wrote that "an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works." Mehta dismissed without prejudice, so Penske may refile.
Potential Talent Implication: A federal judge would not let Penske use antitrust law to make Google pay for AI summaries of its articles, and for creators whose work feeds AI tools, payment may now depend on a license negotiated up front.
The Facts
  • Ruling: U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Penske Media Corporation's lawsuit against Google on Wednesday (Sept. 30); antitrust laws do not apply to AI Overviews of news articles.
  • Mehta: "Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an 'expectation' that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free. But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works."
  • Penske's claims (filed 2025): Google leverages search by including only publishers that permit AI-summary use; about a fifth of Google searches linking to sites show Overviews; Google should be required to pay publishers to summarize articles or use them to train AI; PMC alleged lost revenue.
  • Co-plaintiff: Chegg, alleging Google illegally scraped its content.
  • Penske owns The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, Variety, Rolling Stone, Gold Derby, Billboard, IndieWire and Artforum.
  • Dismissal was not with prejudice; Penske may refile. PMC, Google and Chegg did not immediately comment.

David Ellison named the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery "Skydance" on X Friday, ahead of the $110 billion merger's expected Oct. 6 close after a year of pursuit and a two-month antitrust delay.
David Ellison announced Friday that the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will be called Skydance once their $110 billion merger closes Oct. 6, following a year-long pursuit and a two-month antitrust delay from 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America. Paramount separately priced $41.4 billion in senior secured notes and an $8.5 billion term loan B to finance the deal.   • Financing: Paramount Skydance Corporation priced $41.4 billion and €885 million in senior secured notes offerings and an $8.5 billion and €850 million term loan B facility (announced via SEC filing Sept. 30, 2026).

Kathleen Kennedy, on Leaving Lucasfilm, Warns the Paramount-WBD Merger Could Mean "Fewer Movies Get Made"
Kathleen Kennedy, who stepped down from Lucasfilm in 2026 after 14 years, told Bloomberg Screentime she feels "a bit of relief" leaving and is "worried" the Paramount-WBD merger will mean "a studio disappear[ing] and fewer movies get made."

She called the Disney deal unambiguously worth it and named relaunching the franchise with "The Force Awakens" and launching "Andor" and "The Mandalorian" as her proudest work, while acknowledging the backlash to "The Acolyte" and her 2017 removal of directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller from "Solo." Asked about the industry's direction, she said she is "worried" about the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger reducing the number of buyers and films made, and that she is still forming a view on AI's role in production.

The Facts

  • On the Paramount-WBD merger: "I think we're all worried about that. To have a studio disappear and fewer movies get made, fewer content gets made. The ability for the studios to be able to scale the work that many of us do. I think that's the biggest worry. We'll see. If it really is 30 movies a year, we'll see."

Disney Cuts a Few Hundred More Jobs, Its Third Round Under Josh D'Amaro, With AI-Driven Automation Named as a Factor
Disney cut a couple hundred employees Tuesday, mostly in tech and HR, its third layoff round in six months under CEO Josh D'Amaro, following an internal memo that cited "automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies."
Disney initiated layoffs affecting roughly a couple hundred employees, concentrated in shared tech and HR functions, Deadline reported, a smaller cut than the two previous rounds this year: 1,000 positions in April and several hundred more in July, mostly at Pixar and National Geographic. Disney Entertainment Television and the motion picture studio are largely exempt from this round. The cuts follow a voluntary early-retirement offer to employees 50 and older with 10+ years of tenure, whose opt-in cooling-off period just ended, and a September 18 internal memo from Chief Legal and Global Affairs Officer Horacio Gutierrez warning of "hard choices" and the division becoming "a much smaller organization" through a "transformation process" that includes "automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies." D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston told shareholders August 5 they remain "highly focused on reducing costs across the enterprise," including "reductions in labor." Disney had 231,000 employees at the end of fiscal 2025.
Potential Talent Implication: Disney naming AI-driven workflow automation as part of the rationale for a third layoff round in six months signals that the cost-cutting lens reaching corporate and legal functions today is explicitly tied to the same technology now being evaluated for production and development workflows.
The Facts
  • Disney cut a couple hundred employees Tuesday, September 29, concentrated in tech and HR; a smaller round than the prior two this year.
  • First round: ~1,000 positions cut in April 2026, D'Amaro's first as CEO. Second round: several hundred more in July 2026, mostly at Pixar and National Geographic.
  • Disney Entertainment Television (undergoing a restructuring under new head Debra OConnell) and the motion picture studio are largely exempt from the current cuts, per Deadline's sources.
  • Disney had 231,000 employees as of the end of fiscal 2025: 172,000 in the U.S., 59,000 elsewhere; 16% part-time, 8% seasonal (largely parks and resorts).
  • The cuts follow a voluntary early-retirement offer to employees at or above director level, 50+, with 10+ years at the company; the opt-in cooling-off period ended the past weekend.
  • A September 18 memo from Chief Legal and Global Affairs Officer Horacio Gutierrez to LGA staff warned of "hard choices" about "staffing investments" and the division becoming "a much smaller organization," describing a "transformation process" including "automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies." The memo was widely shared internally.
  • In their August 5 shareholder letter, D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston said they are "evaluating a variety of levers, including reductions in labor and SG&A."
  • Context: between 2023 and 2025 under Bob Iger, roughly 8,000 Disney employees were let go, yielding $7.5 billion in cost savings, far above Disney's initial forecast; the current D'Amaro-era cuts are a fraction of that scale so far.

Raine Group Nears Exit From Ron Howard and Brian Grazer's Imagine Entertainment
The Raine Group is nearing a sale of its 51% stake in Imagine Entertainment, bought for $100 million in 2016, to a private equity-backed marketing firm, with Grazer personally negotiating the deal.
TheWrap reports three people close to the deal confirmed Raine has accepted a purchase price for its majority stake in Ron Howard and Brian Grazer's Imagine Entertainment, with a close expected within two weeks, though prior Imagine M&A talks have collapsed before. The sale follows Imagine's thin run of hits since the 2000s (its last global theatrical success was 2016's "Inferno") and a strained relationship between Raine and Grazer, who is negotiating the deal himself. A prior planned sale to Centricus Asset Management at a $700 million valuation fell apart in 2024 as investor interest in production companies cooled.
Potential Talent Implication: A new, private-equity-backed owner at Imagine resets who controls the company's overhead, its library monetization and its next production deal, at a moment when comparable shingles (SpringHill, Hartbeat, Hello Sunshine) have all been forced into mergers, downsizing, or unit closures.
The Facts
  • Raine, led by co-founder Joe Ravitch and partner Erik Hodge, is exiting its 51% ownership of Imagine Entertainment, purchased for $100 million in 2016; the buyer is a private-equity-backed marketing firm whose name and the price could not be learned.
  • An Imagine representative called TheWrap's report "factually inaccurate" while declining to give further detail.
  • Imagine has been exploring a sale since at least 2024; a planned $700 million sale to Centricus Asset Management fell apart that year as interest in production companies cooled.
  • China Media Capital invested $100 million alongside Raine in 2016; FountainVest Partners invested another $100 million in 2018. By 2021 Imagine was valued around $850 million.
  • Imagine's last global theatrical hit was 2016's "Inferno"; 2025's "After the Hunt" (Julia Roberts, Andrew Garfield) grossed just $9 million worldwide, and Howard's "Eden" (Sydney Sweeney) made $2.8 million after Vertical picked it up. The last Imagine film to cross $100 million domestically was 2017's "American Made" ($135 million on a $50 million budget).
  • Comparable independent production companies have struggled: LeBron James' SpringHill Company (once valued at $750 million) merged into Fulwell 73 in 2024; Kevin Hart's Hartbeat (once valued at $650 million) has downsized repeatedly; Reese Witherspoon's Hello Sunshine shuttered its kids and family unit in 2023.
  • Howard, 72, is in post-production on the Amazon MGM Afghanistan war drama "Alone at Dawn" (Adam Driver); Grazer, 75, continues producing, including Netflix docs "Marty, Life Is Short" and "Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing." Upcoming Imagine titles: 20th Century's "Whalefall" (October theatrical), Amazon MGM's "How to Rob a Bank" (David Leitch), Netflix's "The Mosquito Bowl" (Pete Berg), and the Apple series "Wild Things" (Andrew Garfield, Jude Law). A Howard-Jim Carrey "Grinch" sequel is in early development.
  • Raine has separately been active in sports and gambling deals, including DraftKings, and most recently a $750 million catalog acquisition fund with Ares for music/artist-management company Firebird.

Donna Langley Says She Won Taylor Sheridan With a Better Film Deal, Not a Bigger One
NBCUniversal's Donna Langley says she pulled Taylor Sheridan from Paramount after a decade by upgrading the film side of his deal, since his existing Paramount film pact was only a weaker first-look arrangement.
Speaking at Bloomberg's Screentime event, NBCUniversal Entertainment chair Donna Langley said she moved on Taylor Sheridan after "disruption and instability" at Paramount, likely referring to the year-long Paramount-Warner Bros. merger process, created an opening. Her pitch centered on film rather than television: Sheridan had a film deal at Paramount, but it was only a first-look arrangement with "not as many teeth to it" as his lucrative TV pact. The film component of his new NBCUniversal deal takes effect in 2026; the TV component follows once he completes his Paramount obligations in 2028. Sheridan, who built the "Yellowstone" TV universe at Paramount, is returning to his film-writing roots with Paramount's upcoming "Call of Duty Movie" and "Sicario 3," both of which he scripted before the move.
Potential Talent Implication: A buyer can out-negotiate an incumbent not by topping the whole deal but by identifying which single component of it is contractually weak, the lesson in how Langley priced the one-third of Sheridan's Paramount pact (film) that actually had room to be beaten.
The Facts
  • Langley said her interest in Sheridan began after she "saw an opportunity" created by "disruption and instability" at Paramount; news of Sheridan's NBCUniversal deal broke in late October 2025, months before David Ellison won the bidding war for Warner Bros. Discovery.
  • Langley: "There's just a moment to kind of look around the marketplace and see if there's a competitive advantage. But really, where I started talking to Taylor was about film, because I knew that he had a film deal at Paramount, but it was a first-look deal. Didn't have as many teeth to it as his television deal."
  • The film component of Sheridan's NBCUniversal deal takes effect in 2026; the TV component follows after he fulfills contractual obligations to Paramount in 2028.
  • Sheridan broke out writing films including "Sicario," "Hell or High Water" and "Wind River" before building a TV franchise at Paramount starting with "Yellowstone" in 2018, which spawned "1923," "The Madison," "Dutton Ranch," "Lioness," "Marshals," "Landman" and "Mayor of Kingstown."
  • Sheridan wrote the scripts for Paramount's upcoming "Call of Duty Movie" and "Sicario 3," both predating his move to NBCUniversal.

Donna Langley Says Universal Is Deliberately Undoing Its Own Short-Window Training
NBCUniversal chairman Donna Langley says Universal's move to a slate-wide 45-day theatrical window is a deliberate effort to "undo the training" it gave audiences with its pandemic-era 17-day PVOD window.
At Bloomberg's Screentime event, Langley said Universal's pivot away from the 17-day premium-VOD window it pioneered with AMC in 2020 (back to a slate-wide 45-day minimum theatrical window announced earlier this year) was driven by conversations with filmmakers and a judgment that a 17-day window undermines the moviegoing habit regardless of a film's individual box office performance. Universal and other studios, including the soon-to-be-merged Paramount-Warner, are converging on a 45-day window to premium on-demand and 90 days to streaming. Langley said the streaming window, not the PVOD window, is the one that most threatens theatrical attendance, calling unlimited in-home streaming access "an all you can eat buffet."
Potential Talent Implication: A filmmaker negotiating window length should treat the 90-day streaming threshold, not the 45-day PVOD threshold, as the term studios now consider load-bearing for theatrical health, since Langley singles it out as the one window "that could really undermine the cinemagoing habit."
The Facts
  • Universal struck a deal with AMC Theatres at the onset of COVID-19 allowing PVOD release as early as 17 days after theatrical, which triggered industry-wide windowing experimentation; Universal announced a slate-wide 45-day minimum theatrical window earlier in 2026, ending that era.
  • Langley: "I began to feel that it was time to try and reestablish that moviegoing habit in our audience, and just the simple math of it is that we can't really do that if we're telling them that it's available in the home in 17 days. It was really about signaling to the audience and trying to undo some of the training that we've done to tell them to kind of wait and watch it on their couch."
  • Universal had previously defended the 17-day PVOD window as reaching different audience types, including cost-conscious families; sources at Universal noted 2024's "The Wild Robot" still grossed $334 million after a 17-day PVOD release.
  • Universal and other studios, including the soon-to-close Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery, are converging on a general standard of 45 days to premium on-demand and 90 days to streaming.
  • Langley: "It's the streaming window that I think is the one to really keep an eye on, and we're all pretty consistent around that. That's the one that could, in my opinion, could really undermine the cinemagoing habit, because it's sort of an all you can eat buffet."

With fewer mega-mergers left to chase after Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery, dealmakers at Raine, Loeb & Loeb and Gerber Kawasaki say capital is shifting toward individual creators, IP, and the infrastructure that scales a one-person YouTube business into a company.

The Facts

  • Hodge: "There's a lot of opportunity around the migration of traditional talent, traditional content, onto YouTube."   • Hodge pointed to Raine's investment in Uncensored, the digital network behind "Piers Morgan Uncensored": "With Piers, there's almost no difference between the show that he has on YouTube and the show that he used to have on Fox or CNN." Morgan's program can also be licensed as traditional TV programming.
  • Kulback said creator businesses that start with one personality and brand deals eventually need more sophisticated infrastructure: commercial executives who can secure larger partnerships, plus consumer-products and live-events expertise.
  • Gerber cited MrBeast as the model of an individual YouTube creator scaling into a broader content and consumer-products business, and said "there are many creators that have huge engagement that still have not even built out real businesses," a potential consolidation opportunity to combine creator-led companies into a more cohesive one.
  • Gerber separately cited his investment in Take-Two Interactive, framing gaming as another area of investor attention as entertainment moves across games, film and TV.
  • Hodge pointed to Mediawan's acquisition of Peter Chernin's North Road Company as M&A driven by access to resources and scale, not cost-cutting.
  • Kulback, who represented Google DeepMind in its research partnership and investment in A24, said emerging AI creator tools are blurring the line between technology IP and content IP, raising copyright, likeness and guild questions.
  • Gerber: "This is the best, most entrepreneurial time that I've ever seen" for creators, citing the combination of YouTube, AI and accessible production tools lowering the barriers to entering Hollywood.

Apple Studios Visual Effects Workers Win Their First IATSE Contract
Apple Studios visual effects workers ratified their first IATSE contract, securing minimum rates, AI protections from the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, employer-paid health and retirement benefits, and overtime and rest protections matching editorial crews.
IATSE announced Apple Studios VFX workers secured their first union contract, following the same path as VFX workers on "Avatar" and at Marvel and Disney, who ratified their first contracts last year. The agreement sets minimum rates per covered title tied to annual increases matching the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, minimum-hour guarantees, pay for all hours worked, overtime including holidays and sixth/seventh workdays, employer-paid Motion Picture Industry health care and pension benefits plus a defined-contribution retirement plan (effective retroactively to all hours worked since January 1), AI protections from the Basic Agreement, turnaround and rest protections matching editorial crews, meal penalties, and hazard pay for dangerous on-set conditions. IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb said VFX workers have long powered major productions "without the union protections afforded to many of their colleagues."
Potential Talent Implication: A second major platform's VFX workforce organizing in successive years, each contract carrying explicit AI guardrails from the Basic Agreement, establishes AI-use protections as a now-standard term below-the-line crews expect on any production regardless of which studio or platform is financing it.
The Facts
  • Apple Studios visual effects workers secured their first IATSE contract, per IATSE's September 30 announcement.
  • Contract establishes minimum rates for every covered title; annual minimum-rate increases match those negotiated in the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement.
  • Workers secured minimum-hour guarantees, pay for all hours worked, and overtime protections including holidays and sixth/seventh workdays.
  • Employer-paid Motion Picture Industry health care, pension benefits, and a defined-contribution retirement savings plan; employer contributions to health/retirement plans apply retroactively to all hours worked since January 1, 2026.
  • Contract incorporates AI protections from the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, plus daily/weekly turnaround and rest protections matching editorial crews, meal penalties for violated lunch breaks, and additional pay for hazardous on-set conditions.
  • IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb: "For too long, visual effects workers have powered some the industry's biggest productions without the union protections afforded to many of their colleagues. It is long past time to fix that."

Endeavor's Audacious Carl Icahn Defense

Icahn's lawyers call the new suit "procedurally bizarre."

The Facts

A Filmmaker Pitched Fox Five Meetings in One, Using AI Budget Math to Do It
FoxNXT chief Jon Flynn says a creative pitched Fox Entertainment a feature using AI tools to rationalize roughly 15% of the budget, then proposed reinvesting those savings into two additional shoot locations, all in one meeting.
Speaking at TheWrap's first AI Creator Day, FoxNXT executive vice president Jon Flynn described an unnamed creative's pitch that combined what would normally be five separate meetings into one, built entirely around AI-driven budget math: the standard budget for the feature, a roughly 15% reduction from AI tools, and a proposal to plow those savings back into production value rather than pocket them as savings. Flynn said this reflects a broader shift among pitching filmmakers, who increasingly frame proposals around AI-enabled cost reallocation (time saved, not just money saved) to fund more ambitious production choices within the same top-line budget.
Potential Talent Implication: As AI-driven savings become a line item studios expect in a pitch, the negotiating question shifts from whether AI is used to who controls the budget it frees up: production value on screen, or the fee and backend in the deal.
The Facts
  • Jon Flynn, EVP and head of FoxNXT (Fox Entertainment's internal AI/next-gen technology studio, launched in April), made the comments during a panel at TheWrap and What's Trending's first AI Creator Day, held Tuesday at UCLA's Ralph Freud Playhouse.
  • Flynn described an unnamed creative who came in with a standard budget figure, told Fox they wanted to use AI tools to "rationalize about 15% of the budget," and proposed reinvesting that 15% into two additional filming locations rather than cutting the top-line number.
  • Flynn said this wasn't a one-off: filmmakers are increasingly pitching with AI-driven budget consciousness built in from the start, including using AI to add effects like explosions or to recreate speculative footage (he cited TMZ's "Celebrity Crime Scene: Princess Diana" special) more cheaply than traditional methods.
  • Flynn, a former head of AI go-to-market strategy for media at Google, said the reframing that matters most is time, not cost: a 20% aggregated time/cost savings on a six-episode series could fund a sixth episode's worth of content within the same budget.

A Federal Judge Just Set Paramount's Theatrical Release Schedule Through 2031
A federal judge approved Paramount's $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery settlement Wednesday, locking in a 30-to-32-film annual quota, 45-day theatrical windows and a $30 million penalty per film missed; the deal closes October 6.
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín entered a consent decree Wednesday settling Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery with the states and the WGA, clearing the last obstacle to a close expected October 6. The combined company must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for two years, then 32 for three more, with minimum wide and independent release counts and at least half produced or jointly produced by the combined studio; it must hold 45-day theatrical windows and a 90-day SVOD holdback. Missing the quota costs $30 million per film, with divestiture of Paramount's Miramax stake possible if the shortfall persists. Separately, the decree requires Paramount and Warner to keep basic-cable negotiations apart (violation risks forced divestiture of BET, VH1 and Comedy Central) and creates a five-member independent board, picked by Paramount, overseeing CBS News and CNN editorial standards. The same day, Paramount confirmed former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz will join as Co-CEO overseeing day-to-day operations and integration, starting October 6.
Potential Talent Implication: The settlement's 45-day theatrical window and per-film release quota now function as a court-enforced floor beneath any filmmaker's distribution negotiation with the combined studio, not merely a marketing promise the studio can quietly shorten.
The Facts
  • U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín entered a consent decree Wednesday, September 30, settling Paramount's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery with the state attorneys general and the WGA; the deal is expected to close October 6.
  • Combined company must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years and 32 for the following three years; must maintain minimum numbers of wide and independent releases; at least half of films must be produced or jointly produced by the combined company.
  • Must keep 45-day theatrical windows and a 90-day SVOD holdback for qualifying films.
  • A $30 million per-film penalty applies for missing the annual quota, with divestiture of Paramount's stake in Miramax in play if the shortfall remains unaddressed.
  • Paramount and Warner Bros. must keep basic-cable negotiations separate; a violation could trigger a forced divestiture of BET, VH1 and Comedy Central, among other channels. CNN and New Line Cinema are not on the table in these divestiture scenarios.
  • The decree creates a five-member independent board, selected by Paramount, overseeing editorial standards at CBS News and CNN.
  • The court declined a temporary restraining order sought by Paramount subscribers who alleged the deal would substantially reduce competition in streaming, news and theatrical distribution.
  • Paramount announced the same day that former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz will serve as Co-CEO of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros., starting October 6 and joining the board; Ellison remains Chairman/CEO focused on long-term strategy and creative direction while Kreiz focuses on day-to-day management and integration.
  • The approval follows Tuesday's announcement that Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland is exiting, with HBO's Casey Bloys expected to take over the combined streaming business.

Paramount Gets the Warner Bros. Merger Without Selling a Thing
Paramount's $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger clears a 12-state settlement with no forced divestitures, a 45-day theatrical window, and CNN under an oversight board the Ellisons themselves will appoint.
Paramount and 12 state attorneys general settled the antitrust suit over its Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, with California's Rob Bonta dropping demands for structural remedies like a CNN sale. The deal requires a five-person CNN/CBS News editorial board appointed by the Ellisons' own board, a $1.5 billion five-year U.S. production commitment, 30 films annually (rising to 32), a 45-day theatrical window, and no requirement to keep headquarters in California. Court approval from Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín is still pending; New Jersey Senator Cory Booker filed a letter opposing the settlement, which Paramount and the states rejected Monday.
Potential Talent Implication: A single Ellison-run studio releasing up to 32 films a year gives talent one fewer real bidder in the U.S. market, and the settlement's rental-term protections for theaters expire after three years.
The Facts
  • Deal value: $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance.
  • Settlement parties: 12 states led by California AG Rob Bonta.
  • No forced divestitures (CNN, Miramax, BET remain with the combined company); a $30 million fine per film under the 30-film annual threshold, and a Miramax divestiture, are the sole breach remedies.
  • Combined company releases at least 30 films/year for two years, then 32/year after; 20% of the slate must carry a budget of $50M+; four films per year must qualify as "independent" (originated outside the combined entity, Disney, Universal or Sony, or based on an original screenplay).
  • Theatrical window: 45 days before PVOD/SVOD; 90 days to Paramount+/SVOD.
  • Rental-term protections (no cost increase to exhibitors) hold for years 1-3 only; the protection lapses in years 4-5, when the combined studio is expected to control roughly 30% of the box office.
  • David Ellison becomes sole CEO of both studios; the studios must negotiate TV network carriage deals separately.
  • WBD shareholders receive $31/share, all cash; deal expected to close October 2026.
  • Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) filed a letter opposing the settlement September 24; Paramount, WBD, and the 12 settling states filed a joint response September 28 calling the objection unpersuasive.

Casey Bloys Wins the Race to Run the Combined WarnerMount Streamer
Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland is exiting effective today, clearing the way for HBO CEO Casey Bloys to run the combined 200-million-subscriber streamer once the $110 billion Warner Bros. Discovery deal closes.
Cindy Holland, who has run Paramount+ and Pluto TV since January 2025, told staff Tuesday that "David is optimizing for HBO stability," ceding the combined-streamer path to HBO Max CEO Casey Bloys. The Facts

Indie Film Buyers Have Money and Audiences. They Don't Have Enough Movies.
Top agents at CAA, UTA, WME, Gersh and 30West say a record $4.7 billion summer box office has buyers hungry for independent films, but rising costs mean there aren't enough movies to sell them.
CAA's Roeg Sutherland estimates 70% of movies in the marketplace are now independently financed even when they carry a studio logo, and buyers are competing for bespoke, festival-style films earlier than ever. Rising below-the-line costs like transport have made U.S. production prohibitively expensive, and the domestic pay-TV market that once gave indies a second life has withered. A new federal bill, introduced September 24, would create a transferable tax credit of 20-30% on labor costs, stackable with state incentives. The Paramount-WBD merger is expected to leave only one of two new specialty labels, Warners' Clockwork or Paramount's Republic Pictures, standing.
Potential Talent Implication: Agents say the fight to lower guaranteed up-front talent fees in favor of performance-based pay has quieted because both sides increasingly agree that just getting the movie made matters more, shifting real leverage in specialty film deals toward structures that pay out on results.
The Facts
  • Summer 2026 box office hit a record $4.7 billion.
  • CAA's Roeg Sutherland: "I would say that 70 percent of the movies in the marketplace are independent, in one form or another... most things right now are being financed by outside money," even when a studio logo appears on the release.
  • Curry Barker's "Obsession," bought by Focus Features out of TIFF for $15 million, went on to gross $519 million globally, the highest-grossing festival acquisition of all time.
  • Olivia Wilde's "The Invite" sold to A24 for a reported $12 million in a Sundance bidding war and grossed $60 million worldwide; Lance Oppenheim's Robert Pattinson-led "Primetime" opened to just above $19 million domestically on a $15 million budget.
  • The Motion Picture Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act, introduced September 24 in the House and Senate, would create a transferable federal tax credit on labor costs (including above-the-line talent) starting at 20%, rising to 30% for indie projects and rural/disaster-zone shoots; stackable with state incentives; $1 million minimum spend.
  • WME's Deb McIntosh argues studios/streamers benefiting from the tax credit should be required to spend a share of content budgets licensing independently produced third-party film and TV to rebuild the post-theatrical secondary licensing market.
  • Paramount-WBD merger settlement commits the combined studio to $5 million annually for an independent-film acquisition fund and four theatrical releases per year of qualifying independent films (5-year term); one dealmaker called the commitment "ridiculous," saying: "I don't blame Paramount. I blame whoever thought this was a useful win for us."
  • The merger is expected to leave one of two new studio-funded specialty labels standing: Warners' Clockwork (led by former Neon CMO Christian Parkes) has acquired Sean Baker's "Ti Amo!," Park Chan-wook's "The Brigands of Rattlecreek" (Matthew McConaughey, Pedro Pascal, Austin Butler, Tang Wei) and "Nasty" (Mary Bronstein/Rose Byrne); Noah Baumbach left Netflix for a first-look deal at Warners under the Clockwork banner.
  • Paramount's Republic Pictures, led by Lia Buman, bought StudioCanal's "The Midnight Library" (Florence Pugh) out of Cannes for $36 million.

Paramount began marketing a $44.4 billion debt offering Monday, split between investment-grade and junk bonds, to fund its Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition while a federal judge still withholds settlement approval.
Paramount is marketing $44.4 billion in debt, about $32 billion investment-grade and the equivalent of $12.4 billion in high-yield bonds, to help fund its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Bank of America and Citigroup hosted calls Monday and racked up enough demand to cover the offering the same day. Ellison Revocable Trust and $250 million from RedBird Capital, both of which assigned their subscription rights to outside parties (sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi and Qatar, and investment bank LionTree), who will receive nonvoting Paramount Class B shares at close. Parrot Analytics, writing in TheWrap, reports that global audience demand for Spanish- and Portuguese-language series rose 25% between 2024 and September 2026, led by markets outside Latin America: South Korea (+243%), Japan (+148%) and China (+119%), with Turkish and Nordic demand also rising. A New Bill Would Let Rights Owners Get Foreign Piracy Sites Blocked in the U.S.
The bipartisan DEFEND IP Act lets content owners ask a judge to designate a foreign piracy site and order U.S. internet providers to block it; AT&T, Charter, Comcast, Cox and Verizon oppose it.
House and Senate sponsors from both parties introduced the DEFEND IP Act on Sept. 24. A judge would decide whether a foreign site has "no commercially significant purpose" other than copyright violation; content owners could then seek an order directing U.S. internet providers to take "reasonable measures" to block it, renewable after 360 days, including for pirated live-event streams. It is the industry's first major site-blocking push since SOPA collapsed nearly 15 years ago. The Common Sense Copyright Coalition, whose members include Comcast, opposes it, citing the Supreme Court's March ruling in Cox v. Sony.
Potential Talent Implication: The order goes to whoever owns the copyright, so creators who hold their own rights would gain a direct remedy against foreign piracy, while talent paid on a studio's backend would depend on the studio choosing to use it.
The Facts
  • Bill: Deterring Extraterritorial Foreign Exploitation of Networks Damaging Intellectual Property (DEFEND IP) Act, introduced Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.
  • Sponsors: Reps. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), Ben Cline (R-VA); Sens. Thom Tillis (R-NC), Chris Coons (D-DE), Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), Adam Schiff (D-CA).
  • Mechanism: a judge designates a "foreign digital piracy site" (one with "no commercially significant purpose or use other than committing a violation of copyright"); the order is subject to renewal after 360 days. Content owners may then seek an order directing service providers to "take reasonable measures to prevent users in the United States" from accessing it.
  • Covers transmission of live events from foreign locations that violate copyright.
  • Applicants must show they are "likely to suffer irreparable harm"; measures must be "technically feasible and effective" and not interfere with lawful content.
  • No mandated technical method; legal immunity for ISPs; applies to large-scale foreign sites.
  • Site-blocking is in use in almost 60 countries, per supporters.
  • Opposition: Common Sense Copyright Coalition (AT&T, Charter, Comcast, Cox, Verizon), citing new burdens on broadband providers and Cox v. Sony (March 2026: an ISP is not liable "for merely providing a service to the general public with knowledge that it will be used by some to infringe copyrights").
  • Lofgren: foreign piracy operations "exploit a loophole in our law."

Sony and Universal Music Group, the two majors that never licensed to Suno, sued again, claiming its new v6 model inherits infringement through user outputs and distillation from earlier models.
Sony Music and Universal Music Group filed another lawsuit against AI music company Suno, The Verge reported Sept. 25. The complaint says Suno's v6 model still infringes because it was trained on user outputs from earlier models built on unlicensed recordings, which it calls "model laundering." Sony also alleges distillation (training a new model to reproduce an older model's results). Suno said v6 was trained on partner-licensed content, user creations and preference signals. Sony and UMG are the holdouts that did not sign licensing deals with Suno.
Potential Talent Implication: If "model laundering" holds, a rights holder's claim follows the work into every later model built from it, which makes a license's reach over successor models and synthetic outputs worth as much as the first training fee.

  • Plaintiffs: Sony and Universal Music Group; defendant: Suno. Complaint shared with The Verge.
  • Claim: v6 is trained on user outputs of prior models, which were trained on unlicensed music "ripped from YouTube and other sources."
  • Complaint: "Training a 'new' model on the outputs of an infringing model does not eliminate the infringement; it launders it [...] V6 is not a fresh start; it is the fruit of the same poisoned tree."
  • Complaint: "even a model not directly trained on Plaintiffs' recordings is informed by, and benefits from, Suno's retained unauthorized copies."
  • Sony further alleges v6 was trained by distillation from earlier "teacher" models.
  • Suno (Rachel Racusen): "v6 was trained on content licensed from our partners, interactions including creations and preference signals from our community, and the accumulated learnings from our team." Suno did not specify whether that included uploaded audio.
  • Sony and UMG "are notable holdouts who did not sign a licensing agreement with Suno."
  • Related (The Verge, Sept. 15): UMG is suing DistroKid for alleged deceptive trade practices and copyright infringement.

The Federal Film Credit Bill Counts Star Salaries Toward the 20 Percent
Sens. Tim Scott and Adam Schiff and four House members introduced a 20% federal credit on U.S. production compensation Thursday, above-the-line salaries included, with 5% uplifts that can reach 30%.
A bipartisan group introduced the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act on Thursday. It pays a 20% credit on compensation tied to a production, excluding residuals, and TheWrap reports that above-the-line salaries count, as they do in the UK and Canada. Uplifts of 5% each, to a 30% ceiling, go to shoots in rural opportunity zones or federal disaster areas (Los Angeles County qualifies until 2030), independent productions, shoots across 10 or more states, and studios that raise domestic output. Credits stack on state incentives. Congress is out until after the midterms; Schiff is aiming for the lame-duck session.
Potential Talent Implication: If the bill passes, a producer earns back 20 percent of star and director salaries, and up to 30 percent on an independent shot in Los Angeles, the same above-the-line credit that sent Barbie and Deadpool & Wolverine to shoot abroad.
The Facts
  • Bill: Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, introduced Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.
  • Co-sponsors: Sens. Tim Scott (R-SC), Adam Schiff (D-CA); Reps. Linda Sanchez (D-CA), Brian Jack (R-GA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), Laura Friedman (D-CA). Other backers: Reps. Judy Chu, David Kustoff, Mike Carey, Tom Suozzi.
  • Base rate: 20% of compensation directly related to a production, excluding residuals (Deadline). TheWrap: above-the-line talent salaries count toward the base.
  • Uplifts (5% each, 30% maximum, per TheWrap): at least 30% of principal photography days in a rural qualified opportunity zone or federally declared disaster area; independent production; at least 50% of principal photography and $10M in qualified compensation across 10 or more states; studio increases domestic productions relative to a historical foreign base amount.
  • L.A. County was declared a federal disaster area in 2025 after the Palisades and Altadena fires and keeps the designation until 2030 (TheWrap).
  • Eligibility: total cost above $1M; 75% of production in the U.S.; post-production and VFX covered; animation covered (TheWrap). Excluded: news, live sports, talk shows, daytime dramas, social media content, advertising, corporate video.
  • Credits transferable; stack on top of state incentives (31 states have them, per TheWrap).
  • Timing: House in recess through the midterms; Schiff said the plan is to pass it in the lame-duck session, possibly attached to a major funding bill. TheWrap: bill would take effect for productions at the start of 2027.
  • TheWrap: the $1M floor excludes microbudget films like Obsession (reported $750,000 budget, more than $500M global).
  • MPA statement: passage "could inject $250 billion into the country's economy and deliver nearly 145,000 new jobs every year."
  • Christopher Nolan (DGA president): "the most significant legislative effort in a generation to promote domestic film and television production."
  • Schiff credited Trump for the momentum and said he worked with the White House, Jon Voight and Spencer Pratt.

Sony Paid for a S.W.A.T. Spinoff Itself and Renewed It Before Starz Did
Sony ordered 10 episodes of S.W.A.T. Exiles with no buyer attached in May 2025, found Starz more than a year later, and has already ordered season two on its own money.
Sony Pictures Television self-financed S.W.A.T. Exiles, the Shemar Moore spinoff, as sole producer and distributor after CBS ended the original in May 2025, TV president Katherine Pope told TheWrap. Shopping it first would have cost the stages and the crew, so Sony greenlit 10 episodes days after the finale and sold it to Starz over a year later. Sony has renewed a second season without a Starz commitment; Starz will decide on its own season two based on new subscribers and engagement. Pope said the model only works on a show "produced at a number," not a $15 million-an-episode series.
Potential Talent Implication: When the studio fronts the money itself, a star and crew keep working instead of waiting years for a buyer, but only on a show made at a fixed number, with the platform's terms set after the risk is taken.
The Facts
  • Original: S.W.A.T. ran eight seasons on CBS, co-produced by Sony Pictures TV and CBS Studios; CBS reversed cancellations after seasons 6 and 7; the finale aired May 2025.
  • CBS passed on the spinoff because it had newer franchises in development (Pope).
  • Sony gave S.W.A.T. Exiles a 10-episode order in May 2025, days after the finale, as sole producer and distributor, keeping the Los Angeles sets and crew.
  • Showrunner: Jason Ning, under an overall deal with Sony. Executive producer Neal Moritz.
  • Distributor: Starz, landed "over a year after Sony's green light." Premieres Friday, September 25, 2026.
  • Sony renewed season two without Starz's commitment. Starz president Alison Hoffman: a season-two decision rests on the show's ability to "attract new subscribers, deepen engagement among existing viewers."
  • Pope: "The No. 1 thing about this model is it has to be able to be produced at a number... It's a big number. It's a lot of risk, but... it's not $15 million dollars an episode."
  • Pope: "TV used to be very much a deficit business and a risk-based business, and we got to... streaming deals where you didn't have to take on risk."
  • Pope said the per-season production number stayed essentially the same season after season.

Paramount's Four-Indie-Films Pledge Counts Any Original Screenplay
The combined company targets $6 billion in annual savings within three years and carries about $80 billion in debt. A missed theatrical target costs $30 million per film.
Paramount's settlement with 12 states requires at least four independent films a year, but the consent decree defines an independent film as any movie based on an original screenplay or simply co-produced by Paramount, TheWrap reported in an analysis Wednesday. The Warner Bros. Discovery deal, expected to close in about two weeks, also requires 30 theatrical films a year for two years and 32 for the three after, with a $30 million penalty per missed film. Experts quoted called the penalties toothless. Paramount already holds overall deals with Jon M. Chu, the Duffer Brothers and James Mangold.

The Facts
  • Output terms: at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years, 32 a year for the next three; at least four a year must be independent films; at least 20% must be blockbusters.
  • Definition: the consent decree defines independent films as movies "based on an original screenplay" or simply co-produced by Paramount (TheWrap's reading).
  • Penalties: $30 million per film that misses the theatrical goal; forced divestiture of the 49% Miramax stake within 12 months, and of BET, Comedy Central, VH1, Smithsonian, Destination America and Science Channel within 120 days, for other breaches.
  • Other commitments: $1.5 billion minimum domestic production investment over five years; keep both studio lots; honor guild agreements; $5 million a year to an independent film fund; $9.5 million a year for training programs. If Congress passes a federal credit, 20% of film production in the U.S. for two years, then 30%.
  • Economics: about $80 billion of combined debt; $6 billion in annual merger savings targeted within three years of close. Deal valued at $110 billion.
  • Jobs: an August analysis for the L.A. County Board of Supervisors put nearly 4,500 local film and TV jobs at risk over three years, plus 2,661 indirect jobs.
  • Overall deals already at Paramount: Jon M. Chu, the Duffer Brothers, James Mangold.

  • Experts told TheWrap the penalties are "toothless" and that "all bets are off" after the five-year commitment period.
